chapters.title: Kinematics
chapters.what: Kinematics describes motion without asking why: position r(t), velocity v = dr/dt, acceleration a = dv/dt, in one, two or three dimensions.
chapters.looks: The trajectory with velocity (amber) and acceleration (rose) arrows at the moving point; in 3D the same flight over the ground with a crosswind.
chapters.change: Turn on drag: the path loses its symmetry and the best angle drops below 45°.
chapters.use: Ballistics, sports, vehicle tracking, robot paths, particle detectors.
misc: At the top of a projectile's path the velocity is horizontal, not zero; the acceleration is still g.
Speed and velocity differ: uniform circular motion accelerates.

examples.title: A projectile in vacuum: R = v₀² sin 2θ / g
examples.world: 20 m/s at 45° flies 40.8 m (no air).

examples.title: Why 45° is best (without air)
examples.world: Complementary angles (30° and 60°) land at the same place.

examples.title: The shot put: released 2.1 m up, the best angle is about 42°
examples.world: A raised release point lowers the optimal angle below 45°.

examples.title: A baseball with air drag flies 96 m, not 153 m
examples.world: Quadratic drag (c/m = 0.0062 /m): the path is shortened and steeper on the way down.

examples.title: Uniform circular motion accelerates toward the centre
examples.world: A centrifuge arm: R = 2 m, ω = 3 rad/s gives |a| = ω²R = 18 m/s².

examples.title: A charged particle spirals along a magnetic field
examples.world: Helical tracks in particle detectors and the aurora: radius 1, pitch step 0.5 per radian.

chapters.title: Newton's laws of motion
chapters.what: F = m a: the net force on a body equals its mass times its acceleration; forces come in equal and opposite pairs acting on different bodies.
chapters.looks: The body with every force drawn at its point of action; in 3D the ramp, the block and the cone of friction.
chapters.change: Raise the push P until the needed friction exceeds μsN: the block starts to move, and friction drops to μkN.
chapters.use: Vehicle design, conveyor ramps, lifting, every structural calculation.
misc: Friction does not always oppose the applied force; it opposes sliding (or its tendency).

examples.title: Sliding down a frictionless incline: a = g sin θ
examples.world: An ideal ramp at 30°: 4.9 m/s² down the slope.

examples.title: Pushing a crate across a floor
examples.world: 50 kg, μs = 0.5, μk = 0.4, pushed with 300 N: it breaks free and accelerates at 2.08 m/s².

examples.title: Pulling a sled with a rope at 30°
examples.world: Lifting on the rope reduces N and so the friction: 20 kg, 100 N, μk = 0.2.

examples.title: A banked curve's design speed
examples.world: R = 100 m banked at 15°: at 16.2 m/s no friction is needed at all.

examples.title: A flat road needs friction to turn
examples.world: 1200 kg at 20 m/s round R = 100 m: friction must supply m v²/R = 4.8 kN toward the centre.

chapters.title: Free-body diagrams
chapters.what: A free-body diagram isolates one body and draws every external force on it. The syllabus builds it in seven layers: scene, selected body, isolated body, forces, axes, components, equations.
chapters.looks: Step the layers slider from 1 to 7 and the picture turns from a photograph into a calculation.
chapters.change: Tilt the slope past the cone's half-angle: the reaction R leaves the friction cone and the block slides.
chapters.use: Every statics and dynamics problem starts here — structures, machines, biomechanics.
misc: Internal forces never appear on the diagram of the whole body.
Choose axes along the motion to get one equation per unknown.

examples.title: Layers 1–2: the scene and the chosen body
examples.world: A loading ramp at 20°: first decide what the body is.

examples.title: Layer 3: every force, where it acts
examples.world: A skier on a 20° slope with waxed skis (μk ≈ 0.05).

examples.title: Layer 4: the friction cone
examples.world: A parked car on a 20% grade (11.3°) with μs = 0.7: the reaction stays well inside the cone.

examples.title: Layers 5–6: axes along the slope, components of the weight
examples.world: mg sin θ drives, mg cos θ presses.

examples.title: Layer 7: the equations of motion
examples.world: A box pushed up a 25° ramp with 120 N: which way does it go?

examples.title: A beam's free-body diagram: supports become reactions
examples.world: A 6 m simply supported beam with 10 kN at mid-span: each support pushes up 5 kN.

chapters.title: Work and energy
chapters.what: Work W = ∫F·dx changes kinetic energy. For conservative forces the work is stored as potential energy V, and E = ½mv² + V stays constant.
chapters.looks: The ball rides on its potential-energy curve; the dashed line is its energy; the bars split E into potential (blue) and kinetic (amber). In 3D the curve is a valley.
chapters.change: Raise the release point above a barrier and the motion changes from trapped oscillation to escape; add damping and it settles in a well.
chapters.use: Roller coasters, pendulums, springs, molecular bonds, orbital mechanics.
misc: Turning points are where E = V, not where V is largest.
Normal forces do no work on a sliding body.

examples.title: A roller coaster on an energy landscape
examples.world: The car can only reach heights where V ≤ E.

examples.title: A pendulum as a ball in a cosine well
examples.world: θ released from 1 rad: the period is 2.139 s (L = 1 m), 7% longer than the small-angle value.

examples.title: A spring launcher: all the stored energy becomes speed
examples.world: V = 500 x² per kg, released at 0.1 m: v = √10 = 3.16 m/s at the bottom.

expect.label: speed at the lowest point √(2(E − V_min))

examples.title: A double well: two stable states
examples.world: Bistable MEMS switches and chemical isomers: V = a(x² − 1)².

examples.title: Friction takes energy out
examples.world: With damping the ball loses energy every swing and settles in the nearest well.

examples.title: Work of a stiffening spring: ∫ F dx
examples.world: F = kx + βx³ (rubber mounts stiffen): work to 0.1 m = k x²/2 + β x⁴/4.

chapters.title: Rotational motion
chapters.what: Rotation has its own versions of mass, force and momentum: moment of inertia I, torque τ, angular momentum L = Iω, with τ = dL/dt.
chapters.looks: Bodies racing down a slope, a wheel with its instantaneous centre, gears meshing, a body tumbling with its ω and L arrows.
chapters.change: Swap shapes: the more mass far from the axis, the slower the roll.
chapters.use: Wheels, flywheels, gearboxes, spacecraft attitude, sport (figure skating, diving).
misc: Mass does not matter in the rolling race, only the shape (I/mr²).
ω and L need not be parallel.

examples.title: The rolling race: the solid sphere wins
examples.world: a = g sin θ/(1 + I/mr²): sphere 2/5, disk 1/2, hollow sphere 2/3, ring 1.

expect.label: solid sphere: a = g sinθ/(1 + I/mr²)

examples.title: A rolling wheel: the top moves at 2v, the contact point is at rest
examples.world: The instantaneous centre of rotation is the contact point.

expect.label: speed of the top point 2 ω r

examples.title: A compound gear train: 1500 → 250 rpm
examples.world: Gearboxes trade speed for torque: (20/40)(15/45) = 1/6.

examples.title: The tennis-racket theorem
examples.world: Spin about the intermediate axis is unstable: the body flips (the Dzhanibekov effect in orbit).

examples.title: Gyroscopic precession of a spinning top
examples.world: Gravity's torque turns L sideways: precession rate ≈ mgl/(I₃ω₃).

chapters.title: Friction
chapters.what: Dry (Coulomb) friction resists sliding up to μsN; once sliding it is μkN. The reaction then lies on the friction cone. A rope over a drum multiplies tension exponentially with the wrap angle.
chapters.looks: The friction cone around the normal (3D) and the rope's tension coloured from blue (low) to red (high) round the drum.
chapters.change: Add wraps to the capstan: each extra turn multiplies the holding power by e^{2πμ}.
chapters.use: Brakes, clutches, belts, bollards and capstans, climbing belays, tyres, screws.
misc: Friction is (to first order) independent of contact area.
A belt holds by its wrap angle, not its length.

examples.title: The angle of repose: tan φ = μs
examples.world: Sand and gravel piles; a block starts to slide at 31° when μs = 0.6.

examples.title: A capstan: 1.5 turns multiply the pull 17 times
examples.world: Sailors hold a ship's line on a bollard with one hand.

examples.title: A belt drive over half a pulley
examples.world: A flat belt with 180° of wrap and μ = 0.3: tight side / slack side = e^{0.3π} = 2.57.

examples.title: A car parked on a 20% grade
examples.world: 1500 kg: friction must supply 2.89 kN; with μs = 0.7 there is a big margin.

examples.title: Static to kinetic: the sudden lurch
examples.world: Once a heavy wardrobe starts moving it is easier to keep moving (μk < μs).

chapters.title: Rigid-body dynamics
chapters.what: A rigid body has 6 degrees of freedom: 3 translations of its centre of mass and 3 rotations. Its rotation obeys Euler's equations I₁ω̇₁ = (I₂ − I₃)ω₂ω₃ (and cyclic) when no torque acts.
chapters.looks: A box tumbling with its body axes, ω (teal) and L (rose, fixed in space); a top precessing with its nutation traced.
chapters.change: Start the spin near the intermediate axis and the body flips periodically; near the largest or smallest axis it stays put.
chapters.use: Satellites and spacecraft attitude, gyroscopes, vehicle rollover, sports.
misc: L is constant in space but ω wanders in the body.
Spin about the intermediate principal axis is unstable.

examples.title: The Dzhanibekov effect
examples.world: A wing nut spun in orbit flips every few seconds (seen on Salyut 7, 1985).

examples.title: Stable spin about the largest axis
examples.world: Spin-stabilised satellites spin about their major axis.

examples.title: A spinning top precesses and nods
examples.world: Gyrocompasses and bicycle wheels: precession ≈ mgl/(I₃ω₃).

expect.label: gyroscopic estimate m g l/(I₃ ω₃)

examples.title: Rolling: the ring loses the race
examples.world: a = g sinθ/2 for a hoop — all its mass is at the rim.

examples.title: General plane motion: the instantaneous centre
examples.world: Every point of a rolling wheel moves as if rotating about the contact point.

chapters.title: Simple harmonic motion
chapters.what: A restoring force proportional to displacement (F = −kx) gives sinusoidal motion at the natural frequency ωn = √(k/m), whatever the amplitude.
chapters.looks: The block on its spring beside its x(t) trace; the pendulum swinging in 2D and 3D.
chapters.change: Raise the pendulum's amplitude: the period grows (a pendulum is only simple-harmonic for small swings).
chapters.use: Clocks, suspensions, musical instruments, seismometers, atomic force microscopes.
misc: The period of a spring–mass system does not depend on g.
A pendulum's period does depend on amplitude — slightly.

A pendulum released from 90°
examples.world: Huygens knew large swings run slow: 2.368 s instead of 2.006 s for L = 1 m.

examples.title: A car's suspension bounces at about 1.6 Hz
examples.world: A quarter-car of 300 kg on a 30 kN/m spring.

examples.title: SHM as a ball in a parabolic well
examples.world: V = 50 x² per kg: period 2π/10 = 0.628 s, independent of the release point.

examples.title: The pendulum in 3D: a spherical pendulum

chapters.title: Damped oscillations
chapters.what: Damping removes energy. With damping ratio ζ < 1 the motion rings down inside an exponential envelope; ζ = 1 returns fastest without overshoot; ζ > 1 creeps back.
chapters.looks: The trace inside its dashed envelope; the phase-space trajectory spirals into the origin.
chapters.change: Sweep c through 2√(km): the ringing stops exactly at critical damping.
chapters.use: Car shock absorbers, door closers, instrument needles, building dampers.
misc: More damping is not always faster: overdamped systems are slow.
Damping lowers the frequency only slightly for small ζ.

examples.title: Underdamped: ζ = 0.1 rings down
examples.world: A lightly damped structure after a knock.

examples.title: Critical damping: the fastest settle
examples.world: Door closers and meter needles are tuned near ζ = 1.

examples.title: Overdamped: creeping back
examples.world: A stiff shock absorber: ζ = 3 returns slowly.

examples.title: A car's shock absorber: ζ ≈ 0.3
examples.world: Comfort vs control: passenger cars sit around ζ = 0.2–0.4.

examples.title: A damped pendulum
examples.world: Air resistance slowly steals a pendulum's energy.
